verdict.failure_analysis: All trials passed all hidden cases, including omitted LI closers, nested lists, incomplete tokens/comments inside the first list, and unsupported markup inside vs. after a closed list. The rendered docs did well in the important places: the WP_HTML_Processor overview directs structure-sensitive work away from WP_HTML_Tag_Processor; the 'scan a region before editing its opener' recipe gives the bookmark, next_token, clean-scan, seek-back, mutate pattern; the 'test subtree membership and direct children' recipe gives the #tag, !is_tag_closer(), depth + 1 test; next_token/get_current_depth explain implied closers and bounded walks; create_fragment/get_last_error/paused_at_incomplete_token explain null creation, unsupported markup, and truncation; get_updated_html is clearly distinguished from serialization. The main near-miss is trial-3's explicit closer match: it worked here, but the docs' safer general rule is to end a subtree scan when depth drops below the opener depth. Another near-miss is that the HTML Processor method reference still exposes many private internals, which did not mislead these trials but increases the chance of future undocumented-method calls.

verdict.failure_analysis: No hidden case failed in any trial: each execution.json reports 7/7 passing with no _doing_it_wrong records. verdict.failure_analysis: All trials passed all 7 hidden cases, so there are no failed hidden cases to attribute to misconceptions. The docs did well in several places: the Tag Processor overview's "Which processor should I use?" section explicitly recommends the Tag Processor for flat, position-based attribute/class edits with byte-precise preservation; the Usage section documents construction with new WP_HTML_Tag_Processor($html); Finding tags documents a plain next_tag() loop over tags and explains that comments/raw-text tag-like content are not matched; the attribute modification section documents remove_attribute() as safe even when absent; get_attribute_names_with_prefix() documents the exact API needed for this task, including lowercase returned names and null when no tag opener is matched; get_updated_html() clearly states it is the correct readback path after queued edits and preserves untouched bytes. Near-misses were minor: the successful candidates all inferred that get_attribute_names_with_prefix('data-track-') is the intended way to distinguish data-track-* from data-track/data-tracker, but the prefix method docs could more explicitly state that the prefix comparison follows normalized lowercase HTML attribute names and is intended for data-/aria-/namespace-style bulk operations. verdict.failure_analysis:
All trials passed all 7 frozen cases, so there are no failed hidden cases to attribute to a misconception. The rendered docs did well on the central task: the HTML Processor overview says to use it when structure or normalized output matters; create_fragment() explains body-fragment parsing and null checks; next_token() explains that the processor visits closers for every opener, including unclosed elements; and serialize_token() explicitly describes the token-rewrite pattern, including skipping tokens to remove wrappers and skipping closing tokens too. The SUP-removal example under serialize_token() was especially effective and general enough for subjects to transfer it to SPAN.

The main near-miss was fallback policy. Trials 1 and 2 used normalize($html) after detecting get_last_error(), while trial 3 returned raw input. Both choices are documented as possible policies, and the docs also warn that they discard accumulated rewrites. The task’s string return type gave subjects no obvious sentinel value, so they chose defensive fallbacks that would violate the rewrite contract on unsupported input even though no frozen case exercised that path.
